facts.label: Which 'ton' the Marvel handbooks use
facts.display: Not defined in the handbooks; the US short ton (2,000 lb) is the likely reading
facts.who_when: OHOTMU Deluxe Edition (1985-88), Master Edition (1990-93), 2004-era power grid
facts.notes: No handbook text searched defines 'ton'. The scales mix pounds and tons in US customary units: Master Edition #8 has 'Peak human (able to lift double one's own body weight to 800 pound range)' and 'Enhanced human (able to lift in the 800 pound to 2 ton range)', and the 2004 grid has 'Superhuman: 800 lbs-25 ton range'. So the short ton (907.18474 kg) is the natural reading, but it is an inference. Both verifiers agree. high_si is the long ton, given as a bound. All handbook conversions in this dataset use the short ton. Also relevant to the engine: handbook strength figures are overhead presses (see ohotmu_lift_definition_overhead_press).

facts.label: Sun Wukong's staff (Ruyi Jingu Bang): stated weight
facts.display: 13,500 jin, about 7.97 t at the Ming jin of 590 g
facts.who_when: Journey to the West, chapter 3 (Ming dynasty novel, 16th c.)
facts.notes: Chapter 3 inscription: '如意金箍棒，重一萬三千五百斤' (Compliant Golden-Hooped Rod, weight 13,500 jin). It is repeated as '如意金箍棒，一萬三千五百斤'. I confirmed both in the Wikisource raw text. The staff is called both '天河定底的神珍鐵' and '天河定底神珍鐵'. Conversion: Wikipedia, citing Elvin (2004), gives the Ming jin as 590 g, so 13,500 x 0.590 = 7,965 kg (Wikipedia rounds to 7,960 kg / 17,550 lb). low_si uses the modern 500 g market jin (6,750 kg) and high_si the 1915 Republic jin of 596.816 g (8,057.016 kg). Both are anachronistic for a Ming text; the 590 g value is the defensible one. A further alternative: the Song/Yuan jin listed at 633 g would give 8,545.5 kg. Anthony Yu's English translation says 'pounds', which understates the mass. Length is a separate fact (ruyi_jingu_bang_length).

sources.title: Wikisource: 西遊記 第003回 (Chinese text)
Wikipedia: Ruyi Jingu Bang
Wikipedia: Chinese units of measurement (jin by dynasty)

facts.label: Sun Wukong's staff: stated length (at rest in the sea-palace)
facts.display: 'More than two zhang long' (二丈有餘長), i.e. more than about 6.0-6.4 m; 'about as thick as a dou measure' (斗來粗)
facts.who_when: Journey to the West, chapter 3 (Ming dynasty novel, 16th c.)
facts.notes: New entry (a verifier noted the conversion was possible). Text: '約有斗來粗，二丈有餘長' (about as thick as a dou measure, more than two zhang long), confirmed in the Wikisource raw text. 1 zhang = 10 chi, and Wikipedia's table gives the Ming chi as 0.3008-0.3190 m, so 2 zhang = 6.016-6.380 m. The text says 'more than', so this is a lower bound whose own value is uncertain within that range. The staff changes size at will, so this is its size when found. The thickness cannot be converted: a dou (斗) is a volume measure, and 'as thick as a dou' is a visual comparison. Combined with the 590 g jin mass (7,965 kg), the implied density is not stated in the text and would be the sim's own derivation.

sources.title: Wikisource: 西遊記 第003回 (Chinese text)
Wikipedia: Chinese units of measurement (Ming chi 0.3008-0.3190 m)

facts.label: Milo of Croton carries a four-year-old bull around the course at Olympia
facts.display: No mass stated
facts.who_when: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 10.412e-f (c. AD 200), citing Theodorus of Hierapolis; Yonge translation 1854
facts.notes: Yonge: 'And once at Olympia he took a four year old bull on his shoulders, and carried it all round the course; and after that he killed it and cut it up, and ate it all up by himself in one day.' Athenaeus also gives variants: Phylarchus has it eaten before an altar, and the Dorieus epigram calls it 'a heifer four years old'. Wikipedia gives Milo fl. 540-511 BC and calls the animal a 'four-year-old cow'. The legend was written down about 700 years later. No ancient mass is given, and no sourced live-weight estimate for an archaic Greek four-year-old bovine was found. 10.412e-f is the standard Stephanus citation; the Perseids page uses Yonge page markers (p. 650).

sources.title: Perseids: Athenaeus Book 10 (Yonge)

facts.who_when: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 1.9.5 (c. AD 95), Butler translation
facts.notes: 'Milo, having accustomed himself to carrying a calf every day, ended by carrying it when grown to a bull.' The Perseids segment spans 1.9.5-1.10.3; 1.9.5 is the conventional citation and is not visually marked on the page. No masses or times are given.
